title: Comments of Equinix Inc. on the PJM Interconnection, LLC filing re Reliability Backstop Procurement to Address Resource Adequacy Concerns Stemming from Large Loads under ER26-3380.

documents.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                BEFORE THE
                  FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION



                                                              )
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.                                   )       Docket No. ER26-3380-000
                                                              )


                   COMMENTS OF EQUINIX INC. ON THE
            PJM INTERCONNECTION, LLC FILING REGARDING ITS
            RELIABILITY BACKSTOP PROCUREMENT TO ADDRESS
       RESOURCE ADEQUACY CONCERNS STEMMING FROM LARGE LOADS

        Equinix Inc. (“Equinix”) is pleased to have this opportunity to contribute its comments in

response to the filing by PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”) entitled “Reliability Backstop

Procurement to Address Resource Adequacy Concerns Stemming From Large Loads” (the “RBP

Filing”), which PJM submitted on July 31, 2026.1 We respectfully provide these comments for

consideration by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“Commission” or “FERC”)

pursuant to Rules 211 and 214 of its Rules of Practice and Procedure, 18 C.F.R. §§ 385.211,

385.214, and the Commission’s notice issued in this docket.2


    I. SUMMARY

        Equinix supports the adoption of the RBP on the timeline proposed by PJM. It is an

urgent and necessary mechanism which, if applied as intended as a one-time backstop, can help


1
  PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., “Reliability Backstop Procurement to Address Resource Adequacy Concerns
Stemming from New Load Adjustments,” Docket No. ER26-3380-000, Transmittal Letter (July 31, 2026)
(“Transmittal”). Capitalized terms not defined herein have the meanings given in the Transmittal, the PJM Open
Access Transmission Tariff (“PJM Tariff”), or the PJM Reliability Assurance Agreement among Load Serving
Entities (“RAA”).
2
  PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket No. ER26-3380-000, Combined Notice of Filings, 91 Fed. Reg. 50,827
(Aug. 6, 2026) (establishing a comment date of August 21, 2026). Equinix filed a timely doc-less motion to
intervene in this proceeding on Thursday, August 6, 2026.
 support much-needed near-term stability for both market and reliability conditions. However,

Equinix believes FERC direction is required to achieve several key objectives: to enable the

bilateral procurement that all parties agree is the preferred path; to ensure the RPB is to truly

function as a backstop, and not the default mechanism; to ensure the RBP is truly a one-time

stabilization measure and not a recurring feature of the PJM market; and to avoid unnecessarily

exacerbating the energy affordability concerns that have driven the extremely high degree of

political and public attention on energy rates.

        Equinix asks that FERC take the following actions:

            1) Direct PJM, before the RBP bid submission window opens, to publish clear and
               complete requirements for demonstrating Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MW,
               including the evidence PJM will accept and the process by which large loads may
               submit that evidence directly;

            2) Direct PJM to provide affected loads sufficient transparency into the Large Load
               Adjustment data underlying RBP cost allocation, subject to appropriate
               confidentiality protections, together with a process to correct demonstrable errors
               or duplication;

            3) Modify the proposed buyer-side RBP Collateral provisions so that collateral is
               calibrated to reasonably foreseeable forward exposure and the forms of credit
               support available under Attachment Q are permitted. PJM expressly consented to
               Commission modification or severance of its Section 205 proposal pursuant to
               NRG Power Marketing, LLC v. FERC.3 The Commission therefore can make this
               discrete modification without rejecting or delaying the RBP. As proposed, the
               $1.5 million/MW requirement and restriction to cash or letters of credit would
               unnecessarily and significantly worsen energy affordability issues;

            4) Make clear that acceptance of the RBP is an extraordinary, one-time response and
               encourage PJM to continue work on durable reforms that allow needed resources
               to be studied, interconnected, permitted, and placed in service on timelines
               consistent with identified reliability needs; and

            5) Require PJM to initiate the process of identifying and evaluating tariff-codified
               mechanisms that can be deployed to address significant and potentially long-
               lasting supply-demand gaps.

v. FERC, 862 F.3d 108 (D.C. Cir. 2017)).


                                                                                                                2
    II. BACKGROUND AND INTEREST OF EQUINIX

       Equinix, based in Redwood City, California, is one of the oldest and largest data center

developers in the world, with data centers across six continents, over 35 countries, and more than

70 metropolitan areas. Private enterprises, network operators, cloud providers, governmental

entities and nonprofits house computing equipment and interconnect with one another within

Equinix’s International Business Exchange (“IBX”) data centers. Many of Equinix’s customers

utilize the computing equipment in our data centers and the interconnection services we provide

to enable critical services, such as emergency response, grid operations, medical information,

and national security. Each individual IBX facility may house as many as 400 co-located

customers. Our IBX data centers range between a few megawatts up to approximately 100 MW,

and average in the mid-30 MWs. Equinix also develops, owns and operates larger xScale data

centers, which can exceed 750 MW. Our xScale data centers serve customers requiring a

significant dedicated proportion, or even the entirety, of these larger facilities. The data centers

Equinix develops, owns and operates are long-lived assets developed against investment

horizons measured in decades rather than quarters.

       Equinix has operated in the PJM Region for decades. Its facilities include the very first

commercial data center in Data Center Alley in Northern Virginia, as well as numerous data

centers in the Chicago area, New Jersey, and Northern Virginia. Equinix takes retail electric

service from Electric Distributors and Load Serving Entities across the PJM Region and, in retail

choice jurisdictions, procures its supply through competitive retail suppliers. Depending on how

Equinix’s procurement of new capacity is credited, Equinix may therefore bear charges resulting

from the RBP as states and Relevant Electric Retail Regulatory Authorities (“RERRAs”) further

allocate them, and could be directly affected by any IRAS load-reduction obligation. Equinix has

no financial interest in the outcome of the RBP as a seller; its interest is entirely on the load side.


                                                                                                       3
              Equinix has always held itself to a high standard of care for the communities it operates

in. Recognizing that more is needed to meet the current moment, Equinix recently memorialized

its practices explicitly through its U.S. Community Principles.4 These principles include

Equinix’s commitment to power responsibility, ensuring it “pays the full cost of its grid

infrastructure needs so costs are not passed to consumers.”5 Equinix does not regard the

reliability consequences of large load growth as someone else’s problem to solve, and it has

committed capital to the long-term arrangements needed for new generating capacity and energy

infrastructure.

             Equinix’s interest in this proceeding is accordingly not in a lower capacity price next

year. It is in the long-term stability, predictability, and durability of the rules that govern

reliability and market conditions, including resource adequacy, across the PJM Region. As a load

that intends to sign long-term supply commitments, Equinix needs to know what those

commitments will provide, what risks will remain, and how to best address those remaining

risks. That is the lens through which Equinix offers the comments that follow.


      III.      INTRODUCTION

             Equinix supports PJM’s RBP approach as a one-time response to a severe resource

adequacy shortfall posing a near-term threat to reliability. Equinix urges the Commission to

accept the RBP on PJM’s proposed timeline while making limited, discrete modifications and

clarifications that will make bilateral procurement more workable and avoid unnecessary

financing costs. Those change can be made without delaying the procurement window or

disturbing the core design of PJM’s proposal.

         Equinix asks the Commission to exercise particularly keen oversight to ensure that the

RBP achieves its objective as a backstop, and does not become not the default procurement

mechanism for new capacity. As PJM describes its intent, the RBP “will only procure the

capacity necessary to cover any remaining shortfall from the 2028/2029 BRA after PJM has

accounted for new capacity being brought by new load.”6 The premise of the design of both the

RBP and the closely-related Interim Resource Adequacy Service (“IRAS”) program7—as well as

the focus of the National Energy Dominance Council / PJM Governors’ Principles8 that

prompted these new programs—is that large loads that bring their own new capacity should

neither be procured for, nor charged for capacity procured for loads that failed to procure for

themselves. Equinix agrees with that premise without reservation, has signed on to the Ratepayer

Protection Pledge,9 and has issued its own U.S. Community Principles10 that hold itself to an

even higher standard of care for its communities, consistent with its nearly 30-year strong track

record. In short, Equinix is among the companies developing new large loads that intends to

cover that load with its own new capacity procurement. The premise only operates, however, if

new large loads can reasonably act on it with confidence.

        Equinix therefore does not ask the Commission to hold the RBP back. It asks the

Commission to condition its acceptance on the following points, none of which would require

any delay in the implementation of the RBP:

        1) Equivalency. Whatever capacity qualifies as Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MW

             under proposed section 18.2 must also qualify to relieve the associated load of
            reduction obligations under IRAS. Equinix recognizes that the Commission is limited
            in this docket to addressing issues raised within the IRAS docket, although PJM has
            throughout its Transmittal Letter acknowledged the interaction of the two programs.
            To the extent that PJM believes its proposed requirements for Qualifying RBP Offset
            UCAP MW would fail to meet the requirements of IRAS, however, that should be
            made clear in this docket, and the Commission should consider whether the
            Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MW definition should be adjusted to address those
            concerns so as to avoid conflicting or incompatible criteria.

        2) Clarity, in time to be useful. The RBP bid submission window is scheduled to close
           three weeks after it opens.11 PJM should be directed to publish, before that window
           opens, the specific evidentiary showing it will accept to verify Qualifying RBP Offset
           UCAP MW, including permissible treatment of commercially sensitive information
           and the process for direct submissions by large loads.

        3) Allocation transparency. Direct PJM to provide affected loads access, subject to
           appropriate confidentiality protections, to the zonal Large Load Adjustment data on
           which their RBP cost allocation will rest and a defined process to correct
           demonstrable errors or duplication.12

        4) Buyer-side collateral. Modify the proposed RBP Collateral provisions so that the
           RBP Credit Rate is calibrated to reasonably foreseeable forward exposure and the
           forms of credit support accepted under Tariff, Attachment Q are available. PJM has
           expressly consented to Commission modification or severance of discrete aspects of
           its Section 205 proposal, so this change can be made without rejecting or delaying the
           RBP.13

        Separately, Equinix encourages the Commission to make clear that acceptance of the

RBP is a response to extraordinary near-term conditions, not an endorsement of recurring

backstop procurements as a substitute for durable market, interconnection, transmission and

other required reforms. PJM and its stakeholders should continue that longer-term work on a

considered schedule rather than waiting for the next emergency.

            These limited requests would preserve PJM's proposed procurement timeline while

ensuring it is reasonably feasible for load to undertake the bilateral procurement PJM intends and

expects to minimize the scope and total cost of the RBP. These requests would also serve to

reduce or eliminate avoidable costs that otherwise would be passed through to customers,

exacerbating energy affordability concerns.


     IV.        COMMENTS

           A.     The RBP Is an Appropriate One-Time Response, but the Commission Should
                  Not Assume Current Conditions are a One-Time Aberration.

           As PJM’s RBP transmittal letter observes, the Commission has long recognized that

where market-design measures alone prove insufficient, it “is willing to consider specific

proposals to provide an appropriate last resort process such as an RTO/ISO administered auction

to create a long-term commitment which can support cost-effective financing where the problem

is projected to be a long-term one.”14 Equinix agrees that the present circumstances fit that

description. Two consecutive auctions have cleared short at the cap; PJM represents that all

evidence points to the December 2026 auction clearing short as well. Equinix accordingly

supports the RBP as a one-time mechanism, and supports PJM’s decision to design a tailored

instrument rather than invoke the Reliability Backstop Auction provisions that have sat unused in

Attachment DD, section 16 for twenty years.15 The existing provisions were built for a different

problem.

           Equinix asks the Commission, however, not to lull itself—or the region—into the belief

that acceptance of the RBP would restore a “Pax PJM” in which supply and demand track one


14
   PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 107 FERC ¶ 61,112, at P 21 (2004), order on reh’g, 110 FERC ¶ 61,053 (2005),
quoted in Transmittal at 27.
15

                                                                                                                   7
 another closely and the annual auction will do the rest. The conditions that produced the current

shortfalls are structural. Supply did grow between the two auctions—by a net 1,294.4 MW ICAP

between the 2027/2028 and 2028/2029 BRAs—but, as PJM puts it, “the addition of new supply

has not kept pace with rapid large load demand growth.”16 Replacement supply arrives on

interconnection, permitting, and construction timelines that no procurement mechanism can

compress below physical limits, while PJM’s own twenty-year forecast continues to project

significant long-term load growth.17 The gap between those two rates is what produced the

2027/2028 and 2028/2029 results, and nothing in the RBP changes either rate.

        Morever, significant increases in demand and significant shortfalls in supply availability

may well occur as a result of multiple factors. While the current supply-demand gap is,

inarguably, predominantly driven by data center growth, other causes of supply-demand

imbalance could yield similarly untenable BRA results, as discussed further herein. A more

thoughtful, advanced preparation that is thoroughly vetted through unrushed stakeholder and

FERC review processes is needed to address the likelihood of significant supply-demand gaps in

the future.

        B.       Bilateral Procurement Is the Most Economic and Most Just and Reasonable
                 Path: the Commission Should Ensure the RBP Does Not Displaces It.

                 1.       RBP Cost Allocation Should Align with Load Procurement of its Own
                          New Capacity.

        The Commission’s long-held cost causation principle requires that “all approved rates

reflect to some degree the costs actually caused by the customer who must pay them.”18 PJM

 invokes that principle in support of its allocation methodology, and correctly observes that

decrementing a zone’s allocation by Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MW “guards against

assigning costs to those who will not benefit from the addition of the new capacity procured

through the RBP.”19 Equinix agrees. The difficulty is that the decrement will operate at the level

of the Electric Distributor zone/area, and the further allocation within the zone is left to states

and RERRAs under mechanisms that, in most jurisdictions, do not yet exist. New Jersey presents

one example of how that allocation can be properly structured with its recent Data Center Fair

Share Act,20 and as PJM notes in its transmittal letter Virginia’s State Corporations Commission

and the Data Center Coalition are collaborating on model tariff language that will hopefully also

help address these questions.21

         Further allocation within each zone is left to states and RERRAs, as necessitated by the

split in jurisdiction between wholesale and retail markets. As a result, the wholesale decrement

alone cannot guarantee that the individual load responsible for qualifying bilateral procurement

receives the corresponding retail benefit.

         Equinix does not ask the Commission to dictate retail allocation. It does ask PJM to

provide states and RERRAs the information needed to implement retail mechanisms consistent

with the RBP's design and cost-causation rationale. In particular, PJM should identify the

Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MW reflected in each zone's decrement and work with state

authorities so those data can be used in retail proceedings. That coordination is important if the

RBP is to encourage bilateral procurement while protecting customers that did not cause the need

        It is one thing to say that cost causation need not be perfect; it is another to socialize,

within a rate class, the costs of either 1) speculation by others onto the members of that class

who behaved responsibly, or 2) large load adjustment calculations that are insufficiently tethered

to reasonable assumptions and calculations. It is certainly true, as PJM asserts, that retail cost

allocation measures are outside of PJM’s wholesale market jurisdiction.22 It is equally true, as

PJM observes,

               “[S]erving emerging large loads while meeting the mandates of the PJM state utility
               commissions will ‘require proactive collaboration among states, industry, and PJM
               to develop standardized regulatory tools and model retail tariff structures that
               individual state commissions may consider as they address the integration of new
               large electric loads.’”23

PJM is launching two tidal waves through its proposed market design changes, waves that would

inevitably flow across the jurisdictional divide and impact the retail markets. The clearly

foreseeable impacts of wholesale market changes on retail market conditions require further

action. At the very least, consistent with the Transmittal’s acknowledgment of the need for

“proactive collaboration,” PJM could convene state actors with relevant jurisdiction to

coordinate efforts. This “proactive collaboration” could help ensure wholesale and retail market

elements flange up with minimal unintended adverse consequences, and better realize the shared

intent of the NCED/PJM Governors’ Principles and of PJM’s RBP filing to 1) incent large loads

to bilateral procurement and 2) minimize energy affordability impacts.

                   2.       Bilateral Procurement Requires Clear, Usable Implementation Rules.

         Equinix asks the Commission to recognize that the RBP’s central design premise—that

load will bring its own capacity—places a responsibility on load, and that load can only be

reasonably expected to discharge that responsibility if four conditions are met:

         •   First, PJM must clearly identify when and how Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MW
             will reduce the RBP procurement attributable to a zone and provide states and
             RERRAs information sufficient to trace that decrement to the procurement that
             created it. Load must be assured that new bilateral capacity procurement will protect
             it from RBP cost allocation. That assurance must be reliable at the level of the
             individual load, not merely at the level of the zone.
         •   Second, load must be assured that the same new capacity procurement credited
             against RPB cost allocation will protect it from IRAS curtailment. As noted above,
             while the Commission is limited in what it can do with respect to IRAS in this docket,
             it can ensure that the definitions applicable to RBP do not conflict with those
             applicable to IRAS. As a practical matter, a load facing an unquantified probability of
             curtailment cannot justify the cost of procuring new capacity: if it may be curtailed
             whether or not it self-supplies, it has insufficient reason to bilateral procurement. The
             two instruments must be read together because, from a load perspective, there is very
             little purpose to considering them separately; protection from RBP cost allocation
             pales in comparison to the risk of significant, lengthy and/or repeated curtailment that
             could challenge continued reliability of the information systems our emergency
             response, financial, medical, security and other sectors- and even grid operations-
             have come to rely upon.
         •   Third, PJM should coordinate with the states and RERRAs responsible for retail
             allocation so they have the information necessary to implement the RBP's cost-
             causation design, and consider a convening to ensure wholesale and retail rate designs
             work as seamlessly together as possible. Again, Equinix does not ask the Commission
             to prescribe a retail rate or allocation methodology; it asks that the wholesale
             construct provide a usable factual foundation for the authorities that must make those
             retail decisions.
         •   Fourth, crediting terms must be defined clearly enough to permit effective,
             manageable procurement by load, including the evidence that must be shown to
             ensure that credit is awarded. The proposed Tariff sets out the elements at a high
             level—a signed bilateral contract of at least five Delivery Years, documentation of an
             expected online date no later than June 1, 2032, and evidence matching the capacity
             to load.24 What it does not supply is the form and detailed content requirements of that
             showing, including what documents PJM will accept, what redactions are permitted,

              what happens when a contract is contingent, and how a load whose Electric
             Distributor declines to report on its behalf can make the showing directly. PJM has
             committed to accept reports from “large loads” among others,25 which Equinix
             appreciates. PJM should be directed to publish the accompanying evidentiary
             specification before the procurement window opens. Moreover, a load that has
             satisfied PJM’s evidentiary standard once should not be required to satisfy a different

                  4.       The Peak Shaving, Five year Minimum Term, and Fixed RBP Credit
                           Level Features Properly Support Bilateral Procurement.

         Peak shaving. Equinix applauds PJM’s recognition, in the second proposed opt-out, that

to the extent load participates in a state-codified peak shaving adjustment program, it has already

addressed that extent of its capacity needs and should not be procured for again.27 That

recognition is sound and should be preserved in the RBP. The Transmittal separately notes that a

zone/area receiving that opt-out may still be subject to load reduction under IRAS.28 While that

issue is not formally before the Commission in this docket, other than the reference in the

Transmittal letter itself, Equinix flags it because 1) the reference threatens to undermine the use

of the Peak Shaving programs to achieve the objectives of the RPB, and 2) the interaction

between a federal curtailment construct and state-codified peak-shaving programs raises distinct

 jurisdictional and policy questions, which Equinix anticipates addressing in the IRAS

proceeding.

          Five-year minimum term. Equinix supports PJM’s selection of a five-Delivery-Year

minimum term for the bilateral contracts and bilateral procurement arrangements that may

generate Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MW.29 The balance PJM strikes is the right one: a five-

year floor is long enough to demonstrate that the capacity has been well-established, is not

transitory, and is likely to be available to support resource adequacy needs even after the initial

contracting term is over. It is also short enough to avoid foreclosing commercially reasonable

structures, as well as avoiding excess costs and financing burdens, all of which would serve to

deter bilateral contracting. A longer minimum would have excluded a meaningful share of the

very bilateral procurement the RBP is designed to encourage.

          Fixing the RBP credited value at the time of procurement. Equinix likewise supports

PJM’s proposal to determine the UCAP value of Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MW using the

applicable ELCC Class Ratings for the 2028/2029 Delivery Year BRA, or unit-specific UCAP

values where no class rating exists, rather than re-rating that capacity annually over the life of the

arrangement.30 Load contracting today cannot price accreditation risk fifteen years forward, and

a floating credit would transfer to load a modeling risk it has no ability to manage. Fixing the

capacity value at the time of procurement solely for purposes of crediting against the RBP and its

cost allocation (and not for operational reliability reasons) is therefore just, reasonable, and an

important feature of making long-term bilateral commitments feasible. Equinix therefore urges

the Commission to preserve this element in the RBP. Equinix anticipates addressing the

 treatment of accreditation under IRAS in the separate IRAS proceeding.

         C.       The Commission Should Modify the Proposed Buyer-Side RBP Collateral
                  Requirement to Avoid Excessive and Unduly Restrictive Requirements.

         PJM proposes to require each LSE allocated RBP cost responsibility to post RBP

Collateral equal to an RBP Credit Rate—set initially at $1.5 million—multiplied by the RBP

UCAP MW committed.31 As proposed, RBP Collateral could take only two forms: a cash deposit

or a letter of credit.32 PJM explains that the $1.5 million figure was chosen to hold collateral

covering “approximately 50% of the notional value of all RBP commitments” from day one.33

Equinix respectfully submits that this requirement as currently framed is not just and reasonable,

for three reasons.

         The Commission can remedy these defects without rejecting or delaying the RBP. PJM

expressly consented to Commission modification or severance of its proposal. That consent is

especially important here: the buyer-side collateral provisions are discrete from the

procurement's core design, and modifying them would leave the RBP otherwise intact while

avoiding an unnecessary financing burden.34

         First, the calibration is disproportionate and internally inconsistent. Sellers—who bear

genuine development, supply chain, and permitting risk and have the most control over those

risks, and whose non-performance is the failure mode PJM says most threatens the region—

would be required to post 20% of three Delivery Years of offer value.35 Buyers, whose obligation

         The RBP will, if accepted, create a second capacity construct that operates alongside the

        The broader lesson is that the RBP addresses an immediate procurement gap neither

eliminates the underlying constraints on bringing new supply to load, nor paves the way for the

mechanisms needed to address future significant supply-demand gaps before they disrupt the

market and in more considered fashion. PJM developed this proposal under acute time pressure

and expressly asked the Commission to modify or sever aspects of the filing as needed to permit

timely acceptance. That flexibility is appropriate for the present filing, but it should not become

the region's default method of addressing future supply-demand imbalances.

        Future imbalances could arise from many sources, including additional load growth,

generation retirements, the unexpected loss of major resources, electrification, or delays in

interconnection, transmission, permitting, supply chains, and construction. It would be prudent to

assume there may very well be a next time, if not many future reoccurrences of similar supply-

demand imbalances to those that resulted in this and the IRAS proceedings. PJM has already

begun a broader inquiry into durable market design, and should be commended for doing so,

especially with respect to its thoughtful and insightful white paper.42 Equinix supports that work

and believes it should include the practical reforms necessary for new resources - including

resources procured bilaterally by large loads - to be studied, interconnected, permitted, and

placed in service on timelines that can actually address identified reliability needs.

V.     CONCLUSION

       Equinix supports the Reliability Backstop Procurement as a one-time mechanism and

urges the Commission to accept it so that the procurement window may open as scheduled.

Equinix respectfully requests, however, that in accepting the RBP, the Commission take the

following discrete actions:


       1) Direct PJM, before the RBP bid submission window opens, to publish clear guidance
          as to the evidence it will accept in support of Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MW,
          including the process for direct submissions by large loads;

       2) Direct PJM to provide affected loads, subject to appropriate confidentiality
          protections, access to the RBP target adjustment data relevant to RBP cost allocation
          and a process to correct demonstrable errors or duplication;

       3) Modify the buyer-side RBP Collateral provisions so that collateral is calibrated to
          reasonably foreseeable forward exposure and the forms of credit support accepted
          under Tariff, Attachment Q are available. PJM expressly consented to Commission
          modification or severance of its Section 205 proposal, so the Commission can make
          this discrete change without rejecting or delaying the RBP;

       4) Make clear that acceptance of the RBP is an extraordinary, one-time response and
          encourage PJM to continue work on durable reforms that allow needed resources to
          be studied, interconnected, permitted, and placed in service on timelines consistent
          with identified reliability needs; and

       5) Require PJM to initiate the process of identifying and evaluating tariff-codified
          mechanisms that can be deployed to address significant and potentially long-lasting
          supply-demand gaps.

Equinix does not ask the Commission in this docket to resolve how bilateral procurement should

be treated under IRAS. Equinix does, however, flag that PJM's objective of encouraging large
